Emotions

Why do I feel anxious for no obvious reason?

Sometimes anxiety comes out of nowhere. Understanding how it feeds itself helps it lose its grip.

You are sitting calmly on the sofa when suddenly you notice your heart racing, a knot in your stomach or a sense that something is wrong. There is no danger in sight. This experience is very common and very unsettling.

The anxiety loop

David Clark's cognitive model of panic describes a loop that repeats: we notice a bodily sensation, such as a palpitation or slight dizziness; we interpret it as a sign of danger ("something's happening to me"); that creates fear, fear increases the sensations, and the sensations confirm the danger. Within minutes, a small signal can turn into a crisis.

Anxiety also does not always have an immediate trigger. It can build up through sustained stress, lack of sleep, too much caffeine or worries we are not consciously attending to. And some causes are medical: thyroid problems, certain medicines or heart rhythm disorders. That is why a medical check is advisable if it is new or intense.

What usually helps

  • Remember that the sensation is unpleasant but not dangerous. An anxiety attack peaks within minutes and then subsides, even if we do nothing.
  • Breathe slowly, lengthening the out-breath, to reduce arousal.
  • Do not flee the situations in which it has happened. Avoiding them brings short-term relief but makes the fear grow.
  • Review your lifestyle: sleep, caffeine, alcohol and physical activity have a big influence.
If attacks keep happening or lead you to avoid places or activities, cognitive behavioural therapy gets very good results. Talk to your GP.

References

  1. Clark, D. M. (1986). A cognitive approach to panic. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 24(4), 461–470.
  2. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2011, actualizada 2020). Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113).
